title: PART I

nodes.title: Boeing Business and Operating Segments
nodes.summary: Boeing describes itself as a major aerospace company organized into three segments. Commercial Airplanes develops and sells passenger and cargo jets, including the 737, 767, 777 and 787, while developing the 777X and 737-7/-10. Defense, Space & Security develops and modifies military aircraft, weapons, rotorcraft, defense and intelligence systems, satellites and space-exploration products. Global Services supports commercial and defense customers with logistics, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, parts, training, documentation, digital solutions and analytics.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: The company owns numerous patents, licenses patents from others, and licenses intellectual property to and from third parties. The U.S. government may use or authorize use of inventions covered by patents developed under government contracts. Unpatented research, development and engineering expertise, trademarks, trade secrets, and other intellectual property also contribute to the business. Although intellectual property is important across its businesses, the company does not expect expiration of any individual right or termination of any individual patent license to materially affect operations.

nodes.title: Human Capital
nodes.summary: Boeing reports approximately 182,000 employees, 14% outside the U.S., including 72,000 union members, with 32 U.S. agreements across nine unions and 18 international representative bodies. It lists major unions, represented workforce shares, agreement locations and expiration dates. IAM strikes in 2024 and 2025 disrupted aircraft production and defense programs, harmed operations and finances, and signal risks from future stoppages. Boeing describes culture transformation, competitive pay and benefits, recognition, training and career development (5.8 million learning hours; 12,000 tuition-assistance users), and its commitment to safety, quality, integrity, sustainability, ethical conduct, employee voice and addressing concerns.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The commercial jet market is highly competitive, with BCA facing Airbus and Chinese entrants; it aims to compete through improved products and processes, cost reductions, and superior aircraft and services. BDS competes with major U.S. defense contractors, SpaceX, and expanding non-U.S. firms, sometimes in competitor teams, and expects strong competition through 2026. Services markets are similarly challenging. BGS provides lifecycle support across commercial and defense programs and plans to grow 2026 market share through customer satisfaction and productivity.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: The company operates in heavily regulated U.S. and international markets. Government contracts may be terminated for convenience, generally with payment for completed work and allowable costs, or for default, potentially limiting payment to accepted work and exposing the company to reprocurement costs and damages. Commercial aircraft must meet aviation safety, production, certification, repair, and operational rules; after the January 2024 737-9 door-plug accident, the FAA increased oversight of Spirit’s quality and safety systems and controls 737 production-rate increases and new lines. Environmental laws cover hazardous materials, waste, remediation, and climate emissions, potentially raising costs and requiring investment; compliance and site-management costs recur, and stricter standards or newly found contamination could materially affect financial results. International sales face U.S. and foreign trade, procurement, investment, currency, political, economic, and earnings-repatriation restrictions and risks.

nodes.title: Raw Materials, Parts and Subassemblies
nodes.summary: The company relies heavily on suppliers and subcontractors for essential materials, parts and subassemblies. Key aerospace materials are aluminum, titanium and composites such as carbon and boron. Alternative sources usually exist, but qualifying them can take a year or more. Many major components and equipment are sole-sourced, and the company works with a small number of sole-source suppliers to maintain continuity.

nodes.title: Suppliers
nodes.summary: Boeing relies on domestic and international suppliers and subcontractors to meet cost, quality, performance, and schedule requirements; despite oversight systems, failures and rising prices can harm products, schedules, profitability, and customer commitments. Affordable energy is also necessary. The business is not materially seasonal. The text points to Part III for executive officer information and gives Boeing’s incorporation history, headquarters, contact details, website, and access to its SEC filings and SEC records. It explains that company communications contain forward-looking statements based on uncertain assumptions, subject to risks that may cause actual results to differ, and disclaims any duty to update them except as required by law.

nodes.title: Boeing Business Disclosures and Forward-Looking Statements
nodes.summary: Supplier and subcontractor failures and rising prices, along with energy availability and cost, can affect Boeing’s quality, schedules, profitability, and customer commitments. Its business is not materially seasonal; executive officers are listed in Part III. Boeing’s incorporation history, headquarters, contact details, website, report availability, and SEC resources are provided. The page explains how to identify forward-looking statements, their assumptions and uncertainties, risks that may cause actual results to differ, and the company’s limited obligation to update them.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
nodes.summary: The section introduces investment risks and uncertainties that could materially affect the company’s business, financial position, operating results, and cash flows. It advises reviewing the risks alongside the report’s other information, including management’s discussion and consolidated financial statements, and cautions that past results and historical trends may not predict future performance.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Business and Operations
We depend heavily on commercial airlines, subjecting us to unique risks.
key_items: Market conditions have a significant impact on demand for our commercial aircraft and related services

We enter into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which subjects us to losses if we have cost overruns or if increases in our costs exceed the applicable escalation rate
We derive a significant portion of our revenues from a limited number of commercial airlines
nodes.summary: The company’s commercial aircraft business is exposed to airline-market risks: demand depends on economic growth, political stability, traffic trends, and factors such as profitability, financing, geopolitics, competition, fuel and inflation costs, health crises, sustainability, regulation, and reputation. Industry downturns or customer financial problems may reduce, delay, or cancel orders and payments, harming revenue, profits, cash flow, backlog, and deliveries over several years. Fixed-price contracts with indexed escalation also risk losses when costs rise faster than contract adjustments. Revenue depends heavily on a limited number of airlines, whose purchase choices, fleet decisions, consolidation, and financial condition can constrain sales and profits.

nodes.title: Our Commercial Airplanes business depends on our ability to maintain a healthy production system, ensure every airplane in our production system conforms to exacting specifications, achieve planned production rate targets, successfully develop and certify new aircraft or new derivative aircraft, and meet or exceed stringent performance and reliability standards.
key_items: We must minimize disruption caused by production changes, achieve and maintain operational stability and implement productivity improvements to meet customer demand and maintain our profitability
If our commercial aircraft fail to satisfy performance and reliability requirements and/or potentially required sustainability standards, we could face additional costs and/or lower revenues
nodes.summary: Boeing Commercial Airplanes faces risks from complex production, supplier coordination, skilled-labor needs, and evolving regulatory, performance, and reliability requirements. New programs and derivatives, including the 777X and 737-7/-10, have experienced delays, escalating costs, and potential customer remedies; the 777X recorded major reach-forward losses in 2024–25. Planned production increases depend on operational readiness and FAA concurrence, while disruptions, supplier constraints, labor instability, quality issues, and the Spirit acquisition can delay deliveries and harm financial results. Failure to meet aircraft performance, reliability, or sustainability standards could also raise costs or reduce revenue.

nodes.title: Changes in levels of U.S. government defense spending or acquisition priorities, as well as significant delays in U.S. government appropriations, could negatively impact our business, financial position, results of operations and cash flows.
nodes.summary: The company’s substantial reliance on U.S. government defense and agency contracts exposes it to unpredictable defense spending, driven by security, policy, political, economic, legislative, and spending-cap factors. Continuing resolutions can delay programs and contract work, while shutdowns may cause furloughs, payment and delivery delays, certification setbacks, reduced orders, and operational disruption; impacts are uncertain. Changes in agency acquisition priorities, budgets, and the balance among modernization, sustainment, and emerging technologies could reduce, cancel, or delay contracts and opportunities, materially affecting financial results and cash flows. The DoW is also emphasizing affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, and technical-data/software delivery; company or supplier inability to meet evolving requirements could harm revenue and market share.

nodes.title: Our ability to deliver products and services that satisfy customer requirements is heavily dependent on the performance and financial stability of our subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of highly skilled labor, raw materials and other components.
nodes.summary: The company’s ability to meet customer requirements depends on suppliers, subcontractors, skilled labor, raw materials and components. Supplier inflation, resource and labor constraints, quality problems, financial difficulties, delays, and supply-chain disruptions could prevent commitments and harm financial results and cash flows. Shortages, defects, or high prices for materials such as aluminum, titanium, and composites—including due to tariffs or trade restrictions—could delay products or increase costs. Reliance on single-source suppliers heightens the risk that disruptions, including geopolitical events, materially impair delivery or raise operating costs.

nodes.title: Some of our and our suppliers’ workforces are represented by labor unions. Work stoppages by our employees have adversely affected and could continue to adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations and/or cash flows. Future work stoppages by our or our suppliers’ employees could also adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: About 40% of the company’s workforce (approximately 72,000 employees) was union-represented at year-end 2025 under U.S. and international agreements with varying terms. Union relationships and successor agreements are uncertain, and employee votes may reject tentative deals. IAM strikes in 2024 and 2025 halted or disrupted production across commercial, defense, and other programs, materially affecting business and finances. Future stoppages or costly contracts could harm results and cash flows, limit workforce flexibility, divert management, delay production or development, and strain customer relationships; supplier strikes pose similar risks. Engineering employee contracts expire in October 2026.

nodes.title: Competition within our markets and with respect to our products and services may reduce our future contracts and sales.
nodes.summary: Intense competition across BCA, BDS, and BGS may reduce Boeing’s contracts, sales, revenue, and market share. Competitors may have stronger or more specialized capabilities; BCA faces aggressive international rivals, while BDS faces consolidation, shifting defense budgets and priorities, new non-traditional entrants, and customer cost pressures. BGS competes with many of the same U.S. and international firms. Growing international competition and cross-border consolidation, together with U.S. procurement and compliance requirements, may limit cost competitiveness abroad, and successful competition is not assured.

nodes.title: We derive a significant portion of our revenues from non-U.S. sales and are subject to the risks of doing business in other countries, including those related to tariffs, trade restrictions and government actions.
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. customers, including FMS, generated 46% of 2025 revenue and 60% of Commercial Airplanes contract revenue, and are expected to remain significant. International business risks include regulatory and government actions; geopolitical and trade disputes; taxes, tariffs, sanctions, export controls and other restrictions; sourcing and local-content rules; currency fluctuations; political and economic volatility; customer financing and funding uncertainty; reliance on foreign representatives; operational complexity; legal compliance; and crises such as war, terrorism and epidemics. Evolving U.S. tariffs and foreign retaliation could raise costs, weaken demand, delay deliveries or cancel orders. U.S.–China trade tensions led some Chinese customers to pause deliveries in 2025, though deliveries resumed; future delivery or order shortfalls could reduce deliveries and market share. Deteriorating relations, especially with China or the EU, could materially harm financial position, results and cash flows.

nodes.title: We use estimates and make assumptions in accounting for contracts and programs. Changes in our estimates and/or assumptions could adversely affect our future financial results.
nodes.summary: Contract and program accounting relies on significant judgments and estimates about risks, revenues, completion costs and timing, wages, materials, overhead, performance incentives or penalties, claims, and award fees; changes may harm future results. Commercial aircraft program accounting allocates production, tooling, non-recurring, and warranty costs across estimated production quantities and requires forecasts of units, duration, prices, and costs. These estimates are affected by demand and orders, product mix, production rates and learning, inflation, derivatives, suppliers, negotiations, claims, and certification timing or requirements. Materially different assumptions or circumstances can change reported revenue and profit; further accounting-policy detail is referenced in the Form 10-K.

nodes.title: We may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/strategic alliances or divestitures.
nodes.summary: Mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, alliances, and divestitures may fail to deliver expected benefits or harm financial results due to integration and performance problems, legacy liabilities, cybersecurity risks, transaction and intangible-related costs, impairments, guarantees, partner issues, or indemnification obligations. Integrating the Spirit Acquisition may delay or prevent expected synergies and safety and quality improvements, create operational challenges and expenses, and divert management attention. Joint-venture consolidations may affect reported results. Divestitures, including parts of Digital Aviation Solutions, can create reliance on third parties and service or financial obligations; failures or claims could adversely affect the business and financial condition, including obligations to buyers such as Airbus.

The section covers risks from airline-market dependence and customer concentration; production, quality, certification, rate, performance and reliability challenges; fluctuating U.S. defense spending, appropriations and acquisition priorities; supplier, labor, material and workforce disruptions; intense competition; international sales, geopolitical, trade, regulatory and currency exposure; uncertainty in contract and program estimates; and failure to realize benefits or avoid costs and liabilities from acquisitions, joint ventures, alliances and divestitures. These risks could delay or reduce orders and deliveries and adversely affect revenue, profits, cash flows and market share.

nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from reliance on U.S. government contracts (35% of 2025 revenue), including costly procurement and disclosure rules, contract changes or cancellations, funding cuts, audits, repayment demands, penalties, suspension, debarment, and reputational harm. Fixed-price contracts (about 60% of BDS and BGS defense revenue) risk overruns, losses, delays, and charges amid technical, supplier, and performance uncertainty; examples include major 2024 BDS program losses. Cost-type contracts (about 40%) risk reduced fees, profits, or cancellation. Satellite in-orbit incentives may be withheld or refunded for up to 15 years if performance requirements are unmet.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Technology, Security and Business Disruptions
key_items: Managing a complex, global IT infrastructure exposes us to a variety of risks that could negatively impact our business.
Compromised or unauthorized access of our, our customers’ and/or our suppliers’ systems or data could negatively impact our business.
Business disruptions could seriously affect our future sales and financial condition or increase our costs and expenses.
nodes.summary: The company’s complex, decentralized global IT infrastructure creates risks of inefficiency, cost increases, operational disruption, errors, fraud, regulatory noncompliance, unauthorized access, breaches, and privacy violations. Evolving cyber threats—including attacks by sophisticated actors and through suppliers or service providers—could expose sensitive data or intellectual property, disrupt or compromise operations, products, and services, and cause reputational, regulatory, financial, or business harm. Existing safeguards may fail to prevent, detect, or respond adequately; incidents have occurred and may recur, including affecting customer and supplier information the company manages. Physical security threats, IT failures, extreme weather, natural disasters, pandemics, and other disruptions may interrupt company or supplier operations, delay deliveries, reduce sales, increase costs, and harm reputation.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Matters
key_items: The outcome of litigation and of government inquiries and investigations involving our business is unpredictable, and an adverse decision in any such matter could have a material effect on our financial position, results of operations and cash flows.
Our operations expose us to the risk of material environmental liabilities.
We may be adversely affected by global climate change or by legal, regulatory or market responses to such change.
nodes.summary: The text outlines legal, regulatory, environmental, and climate-related risks. Litigation, government inquiries, or investigations may divert resources and lead to adverse financial, operational, cash-flow, or reputational effects. Environmental laws may expose the company to cleanup costs, penalties, claims, and additional liabilities from stricter rules, enforcement, or newly discovered contamination. Climate change and related physical, regulatory, market, and stakeholder pressures may raise costs, disrupt supply and production, constrain products, and harm competitiveness or reputation. Failure to meet or adequately report public sustainability goals may also damage reputation or access to capital.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity
We may be unable to effectively manage our liquidity, which could adversely affect our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The company’s substantial debt, upcoming principal repayments, aircraft financing commitments, and potential preferred-stock dividends create significant liquidity needs. If additional funding is required, it may need to refinance debt, delay investments, or issue securities on unfavorable or dilutive terms; inability to access sufficient capital affordably could harm its business and financial results. Credit-rating downgrades, market disruption, weaker performance or outlook, production delays, or changing demand could raise borrowing costs and restrict financing access. Investment-grade status and future access to capital markets are not assured.

nodes.title: Pension Obligations and Insurance Risks
key_items: Substantial pension and other postretirement benefit obligations have a material impact on our earnings, shareholders’ equity and cash flows from operations, and could have significant adverse impacts in future periods.
Our insurance coverage may be inadequate to cover all significant risk exposures.
nodes.summary: Defined-benefit pension and postretirement health obligations can materially affect earnings, equity, operating cash flows, future contributions, and government contract profitability. Funding and costs depend on assumptions such as discount rates, asset returns, and medical inflation; changes may have significant financial effects. The company’s insurance and government indemnification may not cover all liabilities, particularly risks from specialized products and technologies. U.S. SAFETY Act protections apply to some products domestically but not internationally, leaving potential substantial exposure.

nodes.title: Common Stock Dilution and Preferred Stock Priority
key_items: The issuance of our common stock upon conversion of our Mandatory convertible preferred stock, and the exchange of the Spirit Exchangeable Notes, as well as any other issuances of our common stock, could dilute the interests of our existing shareholders.
Our common stock ranks junior to the Mandatory convertible preferred stock with respect to dividends and amounts payable in the event of our liquidation, dissolution or winding-up of our affairs.
nodes.summary: Common stock issuances from mandatory preferred stock conversions, exchange of $230 million in Spirit Exchangeable Notes, and equity awards could significantly dilute existing shareholders. Preferred shares automatically convert around October 15, 2027, into 5.8280–6.9940 common shares each; holders may convert earlier at the minimum rate, subject to adjustments. Common stock ranks behind preferred stock for dividends and liquidation distributions: dividends generally cannot be paid until preferred dividends are paid or reserved, and preferred holders must receive $1,000 per share plus accumulated unpaid dividends before common shareholders receive liquidation assets.

The section covers risks from substantial debt, repayments, aircraft commitments and preferred dividends that may strain liquidity and force costly refinancing, delayed investment or dilutive securities issuance; credit downgrades, market disruption and weaker performance could further limit affordable financing. Pension and postretirement obligations depend on uncertain assumptions and may affect earnings, cash flow and contract profitability, while insurance and indemnification may not cover product liabilities, especially internationally. Preferred conversions, exchangeable notes and equity awards may dilute common shareholders, whose dividend and liquidation rights rank behind preferred stock.

Item 1C. Cybersecurity

nodes.title: Risk Management and Strategy
nodes.summary: The company’s cybersecurity strategy uses risk-based technical, policy, monitoring, training, contractual, third-party and oversight measures, informed by NIST and other standards, audits, threat intelligence, benchmarking and partnerships. Safeguards, monitoring, incident plans, testing, simulations and annual employee training support resilience; cyber risks are integrated into enterprise and compliance risk programs overseen by the Board, with consultants providing assistance. A cross-functional supplier-risk program assesses select providers and generally requires industry-standard controls. Past incidents have not materially affected the company, but future incidents could, including through suppliers.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.summary: The Board oversees risk, delegating cybersecurity oversight to the Audit and Aerospace Safety Committees, which report to the full Board. The Audit Committee reviews cybersecurity risk processes, receives bimonthly briefings on risks, threats, incidents, mitigation investments, and governance, and assigns an expert member to review strategy and progress. Potentially material incidents prompt notification of its Chair and possible committee or Board meetings. The Aerospace Safety Committee monitors threats affecting aerospace product safety through management updates. The Board also receives annual briefings. Management’s Global Security Governance Council coordinates enterprise cybersecurity policy, strategy, prevention, detection, mitigation, and remediation. Chaired by experienced CSO Terry Rice, who reports to the CIDO and meets with senior management and the Audit Committee, it includes senior leaders spanning technology, engineering, safety, and product security. The Council tracks objectives with the Executive Council, while security, audit, and legal teams coordinate timely issue resolution and required regulatory reporting.

The page summarizes space by business, lists major locations, and notes shared airport runways and taxiways used under long-term agreements, plus government-furnished facilities. nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: The company is a global aerospace leader with U.S.-centered operations and an extensive international partner network, organized around Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, and Global Services. The 2024 737-9 door-plug accident led to FAA oversight, production slowdowns, and safety and quality improvements, materially affecting 2024–2025 finances. Labor stoppages affecting commercial and defense production ended in November 2024 and November 2025; production resumed or operations normalized, while engineering union contracts expire in October 2026. In late 2025, Boeing sold part of Digital Aviation Solutions for $10.55 billion and acquired Spirit AeroSystems through a share exchange, assuming or repaying debt and bringing in Boeing-related manufacturing, defense, aftermarket, Belfast operations, and about 15,000 employees.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: In 2025, air traffic grew near historical rates, led by international demand and China, while North American low-cost demand stagnated; aircraft demand exceeds supply. Supply chains are improving but inflation and remaining disruptions weigh on productivity and financial results. Airline profits and the industry outlook are stabilizing, though costs and economic, geopolitical, and other uncertainties persist. Long-term travel growth supports projected fleet expansion and demand for about 43,600 aircraft over 20 years, subject to significant external risks. BDS sees strong security-driven demand but faces development-program challenges and lingering margin and cash-flow effects; BGS expects strong commercial revenues and stable government-services demand.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BDS reports strong U.S. and international demand amid security priorities, but fixed-price development challenges have caused earnings charges, while supply-chain stabilization has not yet offset past margin and cash-flow impacts. BGS expects continued commercial revenue growth and stable government-services demand. Consolidated results show 2025 revenue of $89.463 billion, GAAP operating earnings of $4.281 billion, a 4.8% margin, net earnings of $2.235 billion, and diluted EPS of $2.48; non-GAAP core operating earnings were $3.236 billion, a 3.6% margin, and core EPS $1.19. 2024 and 2023 results were losses. Non-GAAP measures exclude certain pension and postretirement costs. Revenue rose $22.946 billion in 2025 versus 2024, led by higher BCA deliveries, BDS volume and fewer unfavorable contract adjustments, and BGS services. Revenue fell $11.277 billion in 2024 versus 2023, as lower BCA deliveries and 737-9 grounding-related considerations and unfavorable BDS contract adjustments outweighed BGS commercial-services growth.

nodes.title: Earnings/(Loss) From Operations
nodes.summary: The table reports 2023–2025 GAAP operating earnings/loss by segment, unallocated items, pension and postretirement FAS/CAS adjustments, and non-GAAP core operating results; notes define the adjustment and core measure. Operating earnings improved $14.988 billion in 2025 versus 2024, driven by BGS’s divestiture gain, lower BDS contract losses, and improved BCA deliveries, partly offset by higher unallocated expenses. Losses worsened $9.934 billion in 2024 versus 2023, mainly from BCA production, program, and delivery issues and BDS contract adjustments; BGS improved. Core results followed segment trends, improving $15.047 billion in 2025 and worsening $9.982 billion in 2024.

It explains year-over-year changes, chiefly timing of share-based allocations, stock-price movements, increased enterprise-product development spending, and higher G&A expense, including U.S. Department of Justice agreement charges of $445 million in 2025 and $244 million in 2024. It also presents pension costs allocated to segments, FAS/CAS service-cost adjustments, and net periodic pension benefit costs, which were broadly consistent across the three years, with references to relevant financial-statement notes.

nodes.title: Other Earnings Items
nodes.summary: The table reports Boeing’s 2023–2025 operating results, other income, interest and debt expense, pretax earnings, income taxes, net earnings, noncontrolling interests, and earnings attributable to shareholders. Non-operating pension income fell from $476 million in 2024 to $176 million in 2025, mainly due to lower expected asset returns; its 2024 decline reflected lower returns and higher actuarial-loss amortization, partly offset by lower interest cost. Postretirement income was $19 million, $73 million, and $58 million, respectively, with changes driven by actuarial amortization, interest cost, and prior-service credits. Interest and debt expense rose $46 million in 2025 due to higher average rates and $266 million in 2024 due to higher average debt. The text refers readers to Notes 18 and 6 for postretirement plans and income taxes.

nodes.title: Total Costs and Expenses (“Cost of Sales”)
nodes.summary: Cost of sales includes materials, labor, overhead and subcontracting. BCA mainly uses program accounting, while long-term contract costs are recorded as incurred and spare-parts costs at average cost. Cost of sales rose $16.666 billion in 2025, mainly from higher deliveries and BCA reach-forward losses, partly offset by lower BDS development-program charges; its revenue ratio fell. In 2024, cost of sales fell $1.562 billion as BCA revenue declined, but its revenue ratio rose due to program losses, lower BCA margins and higher BDS charges. R&D expense was $3.615 billion in 2025, down $197 million, mainly due to lower BCA spending; it was $3.812 billion in 2024, up $435 million from 2023, driven by the 777X and enterprise product-development investment.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.summary: The text reports cost of sales and research and development (R&D) expenses. Cost of sales rose $16.666 billion in 2025 versus 2024, mainly from higher deliveries and increased BCA reach-forward losses, partly offset by lower BDS development-program charges; its share of revenue fell due chiefly to those lower charges. In 2024, cost of sales fell $1.562 billion year over year, but its revenue share increased, reflecting 777X/767 losses, lower BCA margins, and higher BDS charges. R&D totaled $3.615 billion in 2025, down $197 million, mainly from lower BCA spending; it was $3.812 billion in 2024, up $435 million from 2023, driven by the BCA 777X program and greater enterprise product-development investment. Segment-level R&D figures are provided for Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Other.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: The table reports backlog by segment and type at December 31, 2025 and 2024. Total backlog rose from $521.3 billion to $682.2 billion, comprising $639.7 billion in contractual backlog and $42.5 billion unobligated in 2025. Contractual backlog excludes options, unexecuted announced orders, terminable orders, and unfunded government contracts; its increase was primarily driven by Commercial Airplanes. Unobligated backlog covers definitive government contracts lacking authorized funding and grew due to Defense, Space & Security. Delivery delays, production disruptions, and delayed 777X, 737-7, or 737-10 entry into service may reduce backlog or cause cancellations.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: The text outlines uncertainty over U.S. government funding and shutdown risks: temporary funding covered selected agencies through January 30, 2026, with some agencies funded through FY26, but a partial shutdown may follow without further legislation, potentially disrupting contracts, orders, operations, and financial results. It describes volatile global trade, evolving tariffs and U.S.-China tensions that have delayed some Chinese aircraft deliveries, and possible material financial effects; the company monitors requirements and mitigates impacts. Supply-chain inflation, disruption, labor instability, tariffs, and supplier financial problems have reduced productivity and contributed to program losses. Commercial aircraft markets are intensely competitive, with about 85% of BCA backlog tied to non-U.S. airlines and ongoing pricing pressure.

nodes.title: Results of Operations

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: The FY26 U.S. budget request proposed $848 billion for DoW and $19 billion for NASA, versus FY25 appropriations of $856 billion and $25 billion. DoW funding was set to lapse January 30, 2026. Spending uncertainty and possible budget or priority changes could delay, reduce, or cancel programs, materially affecting the company’s finances and cash flows. International demand reflects evolving security threats and modernization needs; BDS expects opportunities across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East, and non-U.S. customers represented 26% of its backlog at year-end 2025.

nodes.title: Results of Operations

Revenue improved in 2025 due to fewer unfavorable contract adjustments and higher volume, but declined in 2024 due to such adjustments. Operating losses improved sharply in 2025 as major fixed-price program losses and unfavorable adjustments fell; losses worsened in 2024, detailing charges across five development programs. It refers readers to Note 15 for fixed-price contract discussion and reports equity-method investment income of $21 million, $125 million and $44 million in 2025, 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: BDS Deliveries, Revenues and Operating Losses

BDS revenue rose $3.316 billion in 2025, mainly from fewer unfavorable contract adjustments and higher volume; it fell $1.015 billion in 2024 due to increased adjustments on five major fixed-price development programs. Operating loss improved to $128 million in 2025 from $5.413 billion in 2024, reflecting $5.196 billion fewer unfavorable adjustments, lower program losses—especially on KC-46A—and stronger results in other programs. Loss worsened from $1.764 billion in 2023 to $5.413 billion in 2024, driven by higher adjustments and $5.013 billion in losses across five development programs, detailed by program. The text refers readers to Note 15 for fixed-price contract discussion and reports equity-method investment income of $21 million, $125 million and $44 million in 2025, 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: BDS Backlog and Program Risks
nodes.summary: BDS backlog rose to $84.786 billion at year-end 2025 from $64.023 billion in 2024, reflecting award timing partly offset by revenue on earlier contracts. Development programs face cost, schedule, technical, and quality risks; cost-type contracts may incur reduced fees or cancellation, while fixed-price programs may generate reach-forward losses. Delays or higher completion costs could cause material charges, termination exposure, or future losses despite current estimates. Examples of programs and the Global Services heading are listed.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: BGS serves aerospace markets through distribution, logistics, maintenance, upgrades, training, professional services, and digital solutions. Commercial demand is expected to remain strong as airlines grow, expand fleets, seek efficiency and longer aircraft lives through analytics and predictive maintenance, and outsource spare-parts management. Government-services demand is stable with low 2025 growth; U.S. growth is expected to be flat, non-U.S. fleets to expand faster, and military fleet retirements and replacements to increase service demand, though U.S. budget uncertainty may delay programs. Competition is intense, with pricing pressure and continued importance of global market access. In 2025, revenue rose to $20.923 billion from $19.954 billion, mainly on stronger government and commercial services; 2024 revenue was $19.127 billion. Operating earnings rose to $13.474 billion, largely due to a $9.566 billion divestiture gain; 2024 earnings were $3.618 billion. Contract catch-up adjustment effects are also reported for both years. Backlog increased 39% to $29.720 billion at year-end 2025, mainly due to award timing, partly offset by revenue recognized on older contracts.

nodes.title: BGS Operations, Revenue, and Industry Competition
nodes.summary: Aviation services faces intense domestic and international competition and pricing pressure; global market access is vital to growth and investment returns. BGS revenue was $20.923 billion in 2025, up $969 million, and $19.954 billion in 2024, up $827 million, driven mainly by higher services revenue; contract catch-up impacts were less unfavorable in 2025 but more unfavorable in 2024. Operating earnings were $13.474 billion in 2025, boosted by a $9.566 billion divestiture gain, and $3.618 billion in 2024, up on commercial services. The table also reports 2023 results and annual revenue shares and margins.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: BGS backlog rose 39% to $29.7 billion at year-end 2025, mainly due to award timing. The text summarizes cash flows and liquidity for 2023–2025: operating cash flow improved sharply in 2025 with higher deliveries, lower customer considerations, working-capital gains, and a divestiture gain; 2024’s large outflow reflected production disruptions, lower deliveries, losses, and adverse working capital. Investing cash flow improved in 2025 from divestiture proceeds, while acquisitions and capital spending increased; capital expenditures are expected to rise in 2026. Financing shifted to cash use in 2025 after 2024 equity issuances; debt was about $54 billion, with short-term debt increasing. It also reports supplier-financing balances, employee tax-withholding share transfers, and suspended common dividends.

nodes.title: Capital Resources

It explains pension funding and expected contributions, common-stock funding of 401(k) plans, and recorded and unrecorded purchase obligations, including inventory commitments and $16.4 billion of industrial participation agreements. It also notes off-balance-sheet arrangements and refers readers to financial-statement notes and risk factors.

nodes.title: Commercial Commitments

Aircraft financing covers aircraft on order, under option, proposed in sales campaigns, or delivered and eligible for refinancing, based on estimated earliest funding dates. Customer financing commitments were $15.2 billion in 2025 versus $17.1 billion in 2024. The company expects to avoid funding a significant portion by arranging third-party financing; historically, little has been funded, but greater funding cannot be ruled out. See Note 15.

nodes.title: Core Operating Earnings/(Loss), Core Operating Margins and Core Earnings/(Loss) Per Share

nodes.title: Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Measures to GAAP Measures
nodes.summary: The text reconciles 2023–2025 non-GAAP core operating earnings, margins, and earnings per share to GAAP results, with adjustments for pension/postretirement service costs and income, deferred taxes, and share counts, plus explanatory footnotes. It then describes critical estimates for long-term contracts: performance obligations, revenue and cost assumptions, quarterly reassessment, catch-up adjustments and losses—including major fixed-price development programs and future risks—and the potential earnings impact of changed assumptions. It begins explaining the requirements for program accounting.

nodes.title: Accounting for Long-term Contracts
nodes.summary: The text discusses critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts at BDS and some BGS operations, typically treated as single performance obligations. Revenue, costs, and profit are estimated using contract terms, options, incentives, cost rules, historical trends, and operational and economic factors. Significant estimates are reviewed quarterly; changes cause cumulative catch-up adjustments or immediate reach-forward losses. Such adjustments reduced operating earnings by $1.377 billion in 2025 and increased operating losses by $6.562 billion in 2024 and $2.943 billion in 2023, mainly from named fixed-price development programs, with continuing loss risk. Estimates are judgmental, and a one-point change in 2025 margins on profitable contracts would alter pretax income by about $320 million. The text begins describing program accounting, which requires reliable estimates over a defined program quantity.

nodes.title: Program Accounting
nodes.summary: The text explains critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts and program accounting. Long-term contract revenue, costs, and profit depend on estimates of pricing, costs, risks, and contract terms, reviewed quarterly; estimate changes can trigger cumulative adjustments or immediate losses. It reports 2023–2025 adjustments and key loss-making fixed-price programs, notes future risks, and quantifies sensitivity to margin assumptions. Program accounting estimates production quantities, sales, costs, schedules, and margins, with quarterly reviews and loss recognition rules. It discusses FAA-dependent production increases and certification delays for new aircraft, 2025 charges on the 777X and 767, further-loss risks, and sensitivity of commercial-aircraft earnings to margins.

nodes.title: Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Most employees formerly in defined benefit pension plans have moved to a company-funded defined contribution plan. Annual measurements of pension obligations and assets rely on assumptions, and changes or actual-versus-expected differences can affect expenses, obligations, and shareholders’ equity. A 25-basis-point discount-rate increase or decrease would reduce or raise the projected obligation by $1.185 billion or $1.310 billion, respectively, with no significant pension-cost impact. A 25-basis-point decrease or increase in expected asset returns would raise or lower 2025 pension cost by $134 million. Note 18 provides assumptions for the past three years.

nodes.title: Deferred Income Taxes – Valuation Allowance
nodes.summary: At year-end 2025, the Company reported $21.065 billion in deferred tax assets, $11.420 billion in liabilities, and a $9.754 billion valuation allowance. nodes.title: Market Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page discusses interest rate, foreign currency, and commodity price risks. Foreign currency forwards hedge committed and forecasted receipts and payments; a 10% exchange-rate change would alter unrealized gains by $425 million, offset by changes in hedged transactions, leaving no material combined risk. Commodity swaps and purchase contracts hedge production-related price changes; a 10% commodity price change would alter unrealized gains by $38 million, likewise offset by hedged transactions, with no material combined risk.

GAAP preparation requires estimates and assumptions affecting reported balances, contingencies, revenues, and expenses; actual results may differ. nodes.title: Revenue and Related Cost Recognition
nodes.summary: The text explains revenue, cost, and R&D accounting: aircraft revenue is recognized at delivery using allocated transaction prices and program accounting; long-term contract revenue is recognized over time based on progress, with variable consideration, estimates, cumulative catch-ups, loss provisions, and related payment timing and contract balances. It also covers spare-parts returns and delivery recognition, service revenue, customer concessions and supplier reimbursements, financial-services leases and loans including collectability and residual values, reinsurance revenues and costs, and R&D expense treatment, including customer-funded best-efforts research.

nodes.title: Research and Development

It covers operating-lease revenue, asset depreciation, held-for-sale measurement, and impairment testing. It also describes workers’ compensation reinsurance participation and 2025–2023 revenues and costs, presented net, and research-and-development expense treatment, including customer-funded best-efforts arrangements and bid-and-proposal costs.

nodes.title: Compensation, Tax, and Benefit Plan Policies
nodes.summary: Share-based compensation is measured at grant-date fair value for share-settled awards and reporting-date fair value for cash-settled awards, net of estimated forfeitures, and expensed over the service period. Income tax provisions reflect tax law and rate changes; tax positions use a more-likely-than-not standard, with related liabilities, interest, and penalties recorded, and deferred tax assets reduced by valuation allowances when realization is unlikely. Pension and other retiree benefits, their actuarial assumptions, gains and losses, amortization, and funded status are described. Postemployment benefits are accrued when payment is probable and estimable.

nodes.title: Environmental Remediation and Cash Policies
nodes.summary: The page describes environmental obligations and remediation accounting: the company assesses liabilities and potential recoveries, accrues probable and estimable costs at its best estimate or the low end of a reasonable range, does not discount costs, and records recoveries when probable. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with original maturities of three months or less. Eligible bank balances are aggregated, while negative balances, mainly uncleared checks, are reclassified to Accounts payable; amounts were $127 and $110 at December 31, 2025 and 2024, respectively.

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for inventories, precontract costs, property and equipment, and leases. Inventory costs include program and contract costs subject to recoverability reviews, with provisions for contract or aircraft-program losses, treatment of deferred production costs, supplier advances, impaired stock, and customer early-issue sales consideration. Recoverable precontract costs are capitalized, while start-up or unrecoverable costs are expensed. Property and software costs are depreciated or amortized over stated useful lives; held-for-sale and held-for-use assets follow valuation and impairment rules. Lease classification, asset and liability presentation, and operating-lease balances are described.

nodes.title: Inventory, Precontract Costs, and Property Accounting
nodes.summary: Aircraft and general inventories are measured at cost, subject to net realizable value, with spare parts at average cost; quarterly reviews identify impairment, which is charged to cost of products. Early issue sales consideration reduces revenue upon aircraft delivery and may be written off if unrecoverable. Probable-to-be-recovered precontract costs are capitalized in inventory, except start-up costs; costs are written off if recovery becomes unlikely. Property and equipment are recorded at cost, depreciated over stated useful lives using specified methods, and periodically reviewed. Internal-use and hosted software costs are capitalized and amortized. Assets held for sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair value less selling costs; held-for-use assets are tested for impairment when indicated, based on recoverability and fair value.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.summary: The text explains how leases are identified at inception and where operating and finance lease assets and liabilities are presented in the financial statements. Operating lease assets and liabilities are recognized at commencement using the estimated present value of payments and the incremental borrowing rate; variable payments are expensed as incurred and excluded. Lease terms include extension or termination options when exercise is reasonably certain, and operating lease expense is recognized straight-line. Real property lease and non-lease components are treated as a single lease component.

nodes.title: Asset Retirement Obligations
nodes.summary: The company records known asset retirement obligations whose fair value can be reasonably estimated, including asbestos removal, decommissioning and lease restoration; recorded amounts are immaterial. Known conditional obligations are unrecorded when timing or settlement methods are insufficiently clear to estimate fair value, and will be recorded once estimable. Undiscovered obligations, such as unknown asbestos, are also excluded from the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for goodwill and acquired intangibles: annual and event-driven impairment testing, the April 1, 2025 qualitative assessment and its results, IPR&D recognition and impairment, and useful lives and impairment of finite-lived assets. It also covers accounting and income classification for time deposits, available-for-sale debt securities, equity-method and other equity investments, including impairment reviews. Derivatives are recorded at fair value; cash-flow hedge gains and losses are deferred in comprehensive income then recognized with the hedged transaction, while non-designated derivatives’ fair-value changes are recognized immediately in earnings.

nodes.title: Investment and Derivative Accounting
nodes.summary: Finite-lived acquired intangible assets are amortized over specified useful lives and tested for impairment when indicators arise, with losses measured against fair value if undiscounted cash flows cannot recover carrying value. Investments cover time deposits, available-for-sale debt securities, equity-method and other equity investments, including their measurement, impairment, and cash-flow treatment. Investment income and losses are classified as operating or non-operating. Derivatives are recorded at fair value; cash-flow hedge gains and losses are initially reported in comprehensive income and later reclassified to earnings, while changes for non-designated derivatives enter earnings immediately.

It also describes commercial aircraft trade-in commitments, accounting for estimated value differences and subsequent adverse changes, and valuation based on aircraft attributes, market conditions, resale, leasing, or scrap prospects, updated quarterly.

nodes.title: Warranties, Supplier Penalties, and Guarantees

Supplier penalties are accrued when likely and estimable. nodes.title: Note 2 – Spirit Acquisition
nodes.summary: Boeing completed its Spirit AeroSystems acquisition on December 8, 2025, making Spirit and its subsidiaries part of Boeing and enabling alignment of production systems, safety and quality practices, and workforces. Total consideration was $8.371 billion: $4.704 billion in Boeing shares, $2.571 billion in loans, advances and payments made for Spirit, $948 million for an assumed-note premium, $109 million for share awards, and $39 million for award exchanges. Under the 0.1955 exchange ratio, 117.5 million Spirit shares became 22.98 million Boeing shares. Boeing’s prior funding supported Spirit’s liquidity, production readiness and tooling, and included payment related to Spirit’s concurrent Airbus transaction. Boeing expensed $53 million in acquisition costs; post-acquisition results were immaterial, and comparative pro forma results were impracticable to prepare. The preliminary purchase-price allocation totals $8.371 billion in net assets, including $9.997 billion of goodwill provisionally assigned to BCA; valuations remain subject to adjustment, especially for inventory, property, goodwill, intangibles and off-market contracts. Intangibles mainly concern customer relationships, with a five-year weighted-average life. Accrued liabilities include $1.065 billion for off-market contracts, whose estimated revenue amortization for 2026–2030 is $113 million, $133 million, $129 million, $102 million and $97 million. Boeing expects to finalize allocation within one year; about $30 million of goodwill and intangibles is tax-deductible.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Digital Aviation Solutions Divestiture

The divestiture included the Jeppesen, ForeFlight, AerData, and OzRunways assets and liabilities and generated a $9,566 gain, recorded under Gain on dispositions, net in the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

nodes.title: Note 4 – Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles

Tables show gross carrying amounts and accumulated amortization for finite-lived acquired intangible asset categories in 2025 and 2024. Amortization expense was $204 million in 2025 and $223 million in 2024; estimated annual expense is $197 million in 2026, declining to $144 million in 2030.

nodes.title: Note 5 – Earnings Per Share

Provides 2023–2025 EPS calculation inputs and results, weighted-average shares, and footnotes identifying participating securities and dilutive instruments. nodes.title: Note 6 – Income Taxes

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable and Credit Loss Allowances
key_items: Note 8 – Allowances for Losses on Financial Assets
nodes.summary: Note 7 reports accounts receivable, net, by U.S. government contracts, Commercial Airplanes, Global Services, Defense, Space & Security, and other receivables for 2025 and 2024, after expected-credit-loss allowances; it clarifies the scope of U.S. government contract categories. Note 8 presents 2024 and 2025 allowance rollforwards for financing receivables, unbilled receivables, other current assets, and other assets, detailing beginning balances, estimate changes, write-offs, recoveries, and ending balances.

nodes.title: Note 9 – Inventories
nodes.summary: Note 9 reports inventories at December 31, 2025 and 2024: commercial aircraft programs ($70.785B and $75.192B), long-term contracts, capitalized precontract costs, commercial spares and other materials, totaling $87.550B and $84.679B. Precontract costs include Commercial Crew, T-7A options and KC-46A. It details 737 deferred costs and tooling, expected recovery from firm and future orders; 777X work in process and tooling, 2023 production-pause costs, resumed production, reach-forward losses of $4.899B in 2025 and $3.499B in 2024, risk factors and potential further losses; and 787 deferred costs, supplier advances, tooling, expected recoveries, and abnormal production expenses of $30M, $256M and $1.014B in 2025, 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: Commercial Aircraft Programs
nodes.summary: Note 9 reports inventories of $87.550 billion at December 31, 2025, versus $84.679 billion in 2024, across commercial aircraft programs, long-term contracts, capitalized precontract costs, and spare parts and other materials; precontract costs include Commercial Crew, T-7A options, and KC-46A amounts. It details 737 deferred costs and tooling, expected recovery from firm and future orders; 777X work in process and tooling, its 2023 production pause and abnormal costs, resumed production, reach-forward losses of $4.899 billion in 2025 and $3.499 billion in 2024, and factors that could cause further losses; and 787 deferred costs, supplier advances, tooling, expected recoveries, and abnormal production costs expensed in 2023–2025. Early issue sales consideration credited to airline customers totaled $6.412 billion in 2025 and $5.837 billion in 2024.

nodes.title: Note 10 – Contracts with Customers
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2025, unbilled receivables rose to $9,158 from $8,363 in 2024, mainly due to revenue exceeding billings at BDS and BGS. The text provides balances for long-term-contract unbilled amounts and claims, including current and after-one-year amounts and credit-loss allowances. Commercial incentive receivables due after one year were $89 in 2025 and $63 in 2024; claims are earned amounts with uncertainty over determination or realization. Advances and progress billings fell to $59,404 from $60,333, primarily due to revenue recognized at BDS and BCA. Revenue recognized from beginning-of-year balances was $20,570 in 2025 and $14,516 in 2024.

nodes.title: Note 11 – Financing Receivables and Operating Lease Equipment
nodes.summary: The note reports financing receivables and operating lease equipment balances at December 31, 2025 and 2024, including sales-type lease investments, credit-loss allowances, equipment depreciation, and totals. Financing receivables were fully collected in 2025; remaining arrangements are one- to four-year operating leases, sometimes with extension, termination, or aircraft purchase options. It provides 2024 sales-type lease payment and unearned-income components, confirms no unguaranteed residual assets, and details portfolio concentration by aircraft model. It also reports impairment charges, lease interest and operating income, insignificant variable payments, commencement profits for 2023–2025, and undiscounted operating-lease cash flows by year, with imputed interest and total.

nodes.title: Note 12 – Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 12 reports property, plant and equipment balances at December 31, 2025 and 2024: land, buildings and improvements, machinery and equipment, construction in progress, gross assets, accumulated depreciation, and net totals. It also gives finance-lease right-of-use asset and depreciation amounts, depreciation expense for 2025–2023, non-cash asset acquisitions in 2025 and 2024, and accounts payable for asset purchases at year-end.

nodes.title: Note 13 – Investments
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2025, investments totaled $19.527 billion, up from $13.480 billion in 2024, comprising time deposits, equity-method investments, restricted cash, available-for-sale debt investments, and equity and other investments. Notes disclose equity-method dividends and undistributed earnings, and $689 million of restricted cash held in escrow under a May 2025 DOJ agreement. Cash-flow investment activity primarily involved time deposits and available-for-sale debt; purchases and maturities are reported for 2023–2025. Available-for-sale debt investments are investment grade, have no expected-credit-loss allowance at year-end 2025, and fair value approximates amortized cost.
