nodes.title: Note 14 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 14 reports operating leases for manufacturing and R&D facilities, warehouses, and offices; annual lease and variable expenses, cash payments, and noncash additions or modifications for 2023–2025; 2024–2025 right-of-use assets, current and noncurrent liabilities, weighted-average lease terms and discount rates; balance-sheet classifications; scheduled future payments and imputed interest; and $65 of office leases commencing in 2026 with 1–20-year terms. Note 15 lists 2024–2025 accrued liabilities by category, including compensation, forward-loss recognition, warranties, customer concessions, contracts, environmental costs, interest, retiree benefits, lease liabilities, and other items, with totals of $27,141 and $24,103, respectively.

nodes.title: 737 MAX Customer Concessions and Other Considerations
nodes.summary: The text reports a $443 million 2024 earnings charge, net of insurance recoveries, for customer disruption from the January 2024 737-9 door plug accident and grounding, recorded as a reduction in product sales. 737 MAX concessions liabilities fell from $1.327 billion to $641 million in 2024 and to $383 million in 2025 through payments, in-kind concessions, and estimate changes; $89 million remained under negotiation at year-end 2025, with most expected to be settled through lower delivery payments. Environmental remediation liabilities were $834 million at the start of 2025 and $877 million at year-end; recorded estimates may be exceeded, with high-end estimates exceeding liabilities by $1.171 billion in 2025 and $1.002 billion in 2024. Some remediation costs cannot yet be reasonably estimated; obligations may include site operations and maintenance for up to 30 years. Product warranty liabilities rose from $2.133 billion to $2.797 billion in 2025, reflecting current-delivery additions, payments, estimate changes, and the Spirit acquisition; they were $2.133 billion at the end of 2024.

nodes.title: Customer Concessions, Environmental Liabilities and Warranties
nodes.summary: Tables show 2025 and 2024 changes in 737 MAX customer-concession liabilities, environmental remediation liabilities, and product warranty liabilities. At year-end 2025, $89 million of customer concessions remained under negotiation, with most contracted amounts expected to be settled through lower delivery payments. Environmental liabilities reflect estimated remediation costs, including site operation and maintenance for up to 30 years; actual costs may exceed recorded amounts, some obligations cannot yet be estimated, and the high-end estimates exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,171 million in 2025 and $1,002 million in 2024.

nodes.title: Aircraft and Other Financial Commitments
key_items: Standby Letters of Credit and Surety Bonds
nodes.summary: Describes aircraft trade-in commitments, including exercise assessments, expiration periods, contractual totals, estimated obligations, and aircraft fair values for 2025 and 2024. Reports financing commitments and projected funding dates, including amounts for customers with below-investment-grade credit and the conclusion that no loss reserve is needed. Also notes joint-venture capital contributions and contingent liabilities from standby letters of credit and surety bonds.

nodes.title: COLI and Supply Chain Financing
nodes.summary: McDonnell Douglas merger-related Company Owned Life Insurance obligations remain despite the company no longer using COLI. At year-end 2025 and 2024, policy cash surrender values were $331 million and $342 million, against loans of $303 million and $314 million; these are offset and presented as a net asset. Participating suppliers may receive invoice payments through an intermediary, generally within 30–90 days. The table reports program payables’ opening balances, additions, payment reductions, and closing balances for 2025 and 2024. The company expects changes in financing availability to have no significant liquidity impact.

nodes.title: Government Assistance
nodes.summary: The text details government incentives, including South Carolina grants and Missouri/Texas tax refunds, their accounting, balances, eligibility periods, and potential clawbacks; Queensland grants and a remaining liability; and Industrial Revenue Bond financing, tax benefits, and equal net-reported assets and liabilities. It outlines U.S. government audits of contract costs and possible disallowances, and risks from fixed-price contracts. For the VC-25B, it reports 2025 and 2024 loss increases, causes, planned contract-term changes, and continuing risk. For the KC-46A, it describes the contract scope and production lots, program value, manufacturing structure, and loss increases and causes.

nodes.title: Contract Risks and Industrial Revenue Bonds
nodes.summary: Industrial Revenue Bonds financed property at three sites, provide tax benefits, and are reported net with equal assets and liabilities of $1,054 and $355 in 2025 and 2024. Government contract costs may be audited, disputed, and require reserves, charges, or refunds. Fixed-price development contracts carry cost, schedule, technical, and contractual risks that may cause losses or other exposure. The $4 billion VC-25B program’s reach-forward loss rose by $60 in 2025 and $379 in 2024; supplier costs drove the 2025 increase, while design changes drove the 2024 increase. Contract terms are expected to be reset in early 2026, and further losses remain possible.

nodes.title: KC-46A Tanker
nodes.summary: The text reviews major aerospace programs and severance costs. For the KC-46A, it outlines contract and production quantities, approximately $32 billion in contract value, rising 2025–24 losses, capitalized costs, supplier termination exposure, and risk of further losses. For MQ-25, it covers contract scope and value, loss increases, 2025 assembly and testing, 2026 plans, and continued loss risk. For T-7A, it describes EMD delivery and testing, revised acquisition plans, production orders and options, losses, precontract costs, supplier liabilities, and risk. Commercial Crew covers Starliner flights and anomalies, losses, planned 2026 missions, certification work, and financial exposure. It also reports $295 million in 2024 severance benefits tied to workforce reductions.

nodes.title: MQ-25, T-7A and Commercial Crew Programs
key_items: T-7A Red Hawk EMD Contract & Production Options
nodes.summary: The page reviews contract scope, costs, progress, testing, schedule, and financial risks for three programs. MQ-25: a Navy EMD contract covers seven aircraft and test articles, with added test aircraft, substantial reach-forward losses, assembly and ground testing underway, and remaining work planned for 2026. T-7A: five EMD aircraft were delivered and flight testing continues; an updated acquisition approach and four test vehicles precede production, with 342 aircraft and related services considered probable, alongside losses and supplier commitments. Commercial Crew: Starliner’s uncrewed test succeeded, but the 2024 crewed test returned uncrewed after propulsion anomalies; losses, certification work, and planned 2026 uncrewed and crewed missions are noted. All programs face risk of further losses.

nodes.title: Severance
nodes.summary: In Q4 2024, the Company announced workforce reductions and recorded $295 in severance benefits for employees expected to be involuntarily terminated by the first half of 2025. Packages followed existing compensation and benefits plans. Remaining severance liabilities were $0 at December 31, 2025, and $287 at December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: Note 16 – Arrangements with Off-Balance Sheet Risk
nodes.summary: The company’s off-balance-sheet arrangements primarily involve guarantees. At December 31, 2025, third-party guarantees had maximum potential payments of $186 million, versus $295 million in 2024; estimated collateral/recourse proceeds were $15 million and recorded liabilities were $14 million in both years. Aircraft repurchase commitments, typically exercisable 10–15 years after delivery and conditional on a future aircraft-sale agreement, generally specify prices below expected fair value and rarely become trade-in commitments. Credit guarantees cover lessee or debtor defaults and expire through 2036. Indemnities for certain sold businesses cover pre-closing environmental and other costs indefinitely; future claims and payments cannot be estimated, while probable, estimable liabilities are included in Note 15.

nodes.title: Note 17 – Debt
nodes.summary: Note 17 describes Boeing’s revolving credit facilities, $10 billion of available credit at year-end 2025, covenant compliance, and Spirit Acquisition debt assumed and repaid, including Spirit notes, exchange terms, guarantees, and interest expense, payments, and capitalization for 2023–2025. It presents short-term and total debt balances by category and maturity, scheduled five-year principal payments, and finance lease payments. Note 18 summarizes defined-benefit pension participation, employees’ transition to defined-contribution plans, and trust funding and investment objectives for major pension plans.

nodes.title: Debt Balances and Scheduled Payments
nodes.summary: Reports debt at December 31, 2025 and 2024, including unsecured debt by interest-rate and maturity range, finance lease obligations, other notes, and total debt. Notes that unsecured debt includes $230 million of Spirit Exchangeable Notes assumed in the Spirit Acquisition, exchangeable for Boeing shares and/or cash at Boeing’s election. Provides scheduled debt and other-note principal payments for 2026–2030 and lists finance lease payment categories through thereafter, including total payments and imputed interest.

nodes.title: Note 18 – Postretirement Plans
nodes.summary: Note 18 describes pension and other postretirement benefit (OPB) plans: most employees have moved from defined benefit pensions to company-funded defined contribution savings plans; major pension plans are trust-funded, and OPB mainly provides retiree health care and some life insurance. It explains coverage, funded-status measurement and balance-sheet classification, and a 2025 merger of seven pension plans to use overfunding. Tables report 2023–2025 periodic benefit costs and income, and 2024–2025 changes in obligations, assets, and funded status. The 2025 Spirit Acquisition added three frozen defined benefit plans and two postretirement medical plans.

nodes.title: Pension and OPB Obligations and Plan Assets
nodes.summary: Tables report changes in pension and other postretirement benefit (OPB) obligations, plan assets, and funded status for 2025 and 2024. Obligation balances use pension projected benefit obligations (PBO) and OPB accumulated postretirement benefit obligations (APBO). Obligation changes include opening balance, service and interest costs, amendments, actuarial gains or losses, benefits paid, subsidies, Spirit acquisition, exchange-rate adjustments, and ending balance. Plan asset changes include opening fair value, actual returns, participant contributions, Spirit acquisition, benefits paid, exchange-rate adjustments, and ending fair value.

nodes.title: Amounts recognized in Consolidated Statements of Financial Position at December 31 consist of:
nodes.summary: The text presents year-end 2025 and 2024 pension and other postretirement benefit amounts recognized in the consolidated statements of financial position, including assets, liabilities, and net recognized amounts. It explains that actuarial gains and losses arise from assumption changes, with 2025 pension-obligation losses and 2024 gains primarily due to discount-rate changes. It also reports amounts in accumulated other comprehensive loss (net actuarial losses or gains and prior service credits), total pension accumulated benefit obligations, and the categories of benefit obligations and plan assets for plans whose obligations exceeded their assets.

nodes.title: Assumptions
nodes.summary: The text presents weighted-average assumptions used to calculate benefit obligations and subsequent-year periodic costs, including 2023–2025 discount rates for pension and postretirement benefits, expected asset returns, compensation increases, and cash-balance interest rates. It explains how discount rates are derived from high-quality bond yield curves and applied to projected payments, and how expected returns reflect historical and prospective performance, using a five-year moving-average market-related asset value (about $1,398 above fair value at December 31, 2025). It also introduces assumed health-care cost trend rates.

nodes.title: Plan Assets
Investment Strategy
nodes.summary: The text describes pension asset investment objectives, including meeting benefit obligations, liquidity, competitive returns, diversification, risk management, and reducing asset-liability volatility. Strategic allocations are periodically optimized using liability, liquidity, funding, and return considerations, with de-risking as funding improves; benchmarks, rebalancing, and derivatives help manage allocations. Actual and target 2025/2024 allocations are listed for fixed income, global equity, private equity, real estate/real assets, and hedge funds. It outlines each asset class’s investments and strategies, manager guidelines and permitted derivative uses, and reports derivative net notionals for fixed income and global equity/commodities in 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Risk Management
nodes.summary: Pension asset risk management covers funded status, interest rate, market, counterparty, liquidity, and operational risks. The strategy emphasizes liability matching and diversification across asset classes, strategies, managers, sectors, and holdings. Public-asset manager guidelines are monitored by the custodian, and OTC derivative counterparties are subject to credit limits. Valuation is controlled through reviews of manager and custodian policies and processes, pricing practices and reconciliations, and periodic security-specific testing.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.summary: The text presents pension plan assets’ fair-value hierarchy (Levels 1–3) by investment type for 2025 and 2024, including NAV-practical-expedient investments, cash, receivables and payables. It explains valuation methods and inputs for fixed income, derivatives, cash, equities, private investments, real estate/assets and hedge funds, including lagged NAV adjustments and third-party valuations. It also reconciles Level 3 balances by asset class for both years and reports unrealized gains or losses on Level 3 assets still held at year-end.

nodes.title: OPB Plan Assets
nodes.summary: OPB assets are mainly held in daily-liquid index funds allocated about 60% equity and 40% debt, valued daily at manager-calculated NAV; their returns do not materially affect periodic benefit cost. Required 2026 pension contributions are expected to be insignificant, with no discretionary contributions planned. Expected pension and other postretirement benefit payments for 2026–2035 are listed, including gross benefits, subsidies, and net benefits; OPB figures represent the company’s share only. Certain plans specify asset allocation after an unapproved change of control and termination, and the U.S. government may receive a fair share of surplus assets attributable to reimbursed contract contributions. Defined contribution plans, principally 401(k)s, cost $1,602 million, $1,670 million, and $1,564 million in 2025, 2024, and 2023. The 2023 Incentive Stock Plan authorizes various stock and cash awards and 12.9 million shares plus shares available under the former plan; no further awards may be granted under the 2003 plan.

nodes.title: Pension Benefits and Compensation Plans
nodes.summary: Covers pension investment valuation and expected 2026 contributions; projected pension and postretirement benefit payments for 2026–2035; plan termination provisions involving change of control, ERISA benefits, surplus funding, and U.S. government asset allocation; defined contribution plans and expenses for 2023–2025; and the 2023 Incentive Stock Plan’s eligible awards, share authorization, and replacement of the 2003 plan.

Describes pension plan investment objectives, target and actual allocations, asset-class strategies, benchmarks, derivatives, and risk controls covering funding, market, liquidity, counterparty, operational, and valuation risks. Presents 2025 and 2024 fair-value hierarchies, valuation methods, Level 3 reconciliations, and year-end unrealized results. Also covers OPB assets, expected contributions and 2026–2035 benefit payments, plan termination and surplus provisions, defined contribution plan costs for 2023–2025, and stock-plan awards and share authorizations.

nodes.title: Pension Cash Flows, Termination, and Defined Contribution Plans
nodes.summary: The page notes that commingled funds are valued daily at manager-calculated NAVs and their expected returns do not materially affect pension costs. Required 2026 pension contributions are not expected to be significant, with no discretionary contributions planned. It lists expected pension and other postretirement benefit payments for 2026–2035, including gross benefits, subsidies, and net amounts. Certain plan terminations after an unapproved change in control direct assets first to ERISA-required benefits, then any surplus to a trust for medical and life benefits; excess assets may also require fair allocation to the U.S. government for reimbursed contract contributions. Eligible employees receive defined contribution plans, principally 401(k)s, with expenses of $1,602 million, $1,670 million, and $1,564 million in 2025, 2024, and 2023.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: The text describes the 2023 Incentive Stock Plan, its eligible awards and participants, 12.9 million authorized shares plus carryover shares, the end of grants under the 2003 plan, treasury-share funding, and share-based compensation expenses and tax benefits for 2023–2025. It outlines executive stock-option vesting, expiration and post-termination exercise rules; Monte Carlo valuation assumptions; 2025 premium-priced grants and their terms; and 2025 option activity, outstanding and exercisable balances, values, and exercise-related information for 2023–2025.

nodes.title: Stock Options
nodes.summary: The 2023 Incentive Stock Plan is funded from treasury shares unless insufficient; current holdings are expected to cover 2026 issuances. Share-based compensation expense, mainly in operating and administrative costs with some inventoried in production, and related tax benefits are reported for 2023–2025. Executive stock options generally vest after three years and expire after ten, with certain post-employment exercise eligibility. 2025 grants included premium-priced options at 120% of grant-date fair value; valuation used Monte Carlo assumptions with no dividends. Grant details and 2025 option activity, including balances, exercise prices, remaining life, and intrinsic value, are presented; 2024–2023 grants and 2025–2024 exercises were immaterial. The text also reports 2023 exercise value and tax benefit, unrecognized compensation cost and recognition period at year-end 2025, and vested option fair values for 2025–2024 (none vested in 2023).

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text describes RSU grants to executives in February 2023–2025 and March 2024, their grant-date fair values, and retirement-related vesting rules; other cases forfeit the awards. It also covers 164,806 Boeing RSUs exchanged for Spirit awards in the December 2025 acquisition, including cash-settled units and compensation expense recognition. RSU values generally use the grant-date average high and low stock prices. A 2025 activity table reports beginning, granted, forfeited, distributed, and ending units, vested undistributed units, weighted-average fair values, unrecognized compensation costs, and remaining amortization periods for the Long-Term Incentive Program and Other awards.

nodes.title: Equity Awards and Employee Compensation Plans
nodes.summary: The page describes executive PRSUs granted in 2024 and 2023, their performance-based payouts, vesting, retirement-related eligibility, 2025 forfeitures, and lack of unrecognized compensation cost. It notes that peer-TSR PBRSUs expired with no payout in 2023 and none were outstanding in 2025. The employee stock purchase plan offers shares at a 5% discount and reports authorized shares and 2025 purchases. Deferred compensation plans allow eligible employees to defer pay into 23 investment options; related expense or income and year-end liabilities are reported for 2023–2025.

nodes.title: Shareholders’ Equity and Share Balances
nodes.summary: Note 20 reports that 1.2 billion common shares and 20 million preferred shares were authorized at December 31, 2025 and 2024. A table presents changes in common, treasury, and mandatory convertible preferred shares from January 2023 through December 2025. Disclosures describe 2025 common shares issued from treasury in exchange for Spirit shares in the Spirit Acquisition and 2024 treasury shares issued for net cash proceeds of $18.181 million.

nodes.title: Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock
nodes.summary: On October 31, 2024, the company issued 115 million depositary shares representing 5.75 million 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred shares, with $1,000 liquidation preference and $1 par value, receiving $5,651 net proceeds. Cumulative dividends may be paid in cash, common stock, or both on quarterly dates; payments were $331 in 2025 and zero in 2024, and $86 was declared in December 2025 and paid January 15, 2026. Preferred shares may be converted early at 5.8280 common shares each, subject to adjustments, or automatically convert October 15, 2027, into 5.8280–6.9940 shares based on the common-stock market value. The conversion rate uses a specified 20-trading-day price average and tiered thresholds. A qualifying fundamental change permits conversion at a defined rate and compensation for accumulated and remaining scheduled dividends.

nodes.summary:
Additional Paid-in Capital

During the year ended December 31, 2023, Additional paid-in capital included a decrease of $267 related to a non-cash transaction to purchase shares in a consolidated subsidiary from the noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: AOCI Changes and Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary: Presents accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) movements by component for 2023–2025, including currency translation, investment and derivative gains and losses, and defined benefit pension and postretirement items. Notes explain tax treatment and major pension remeasurements and reclassifications. Describes cash flow hedges using foreign currency forwards for expected sales and purchases through 2032 and commodity swaps and purchase contracts to hedge production input prices through 2029.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments Not Receiving Hedge Accounting Treatment
nodes.summary: The company held foreign currency forwards that did not qualify for hedge accounting. At December 31, 2024, it also had offsetting aluminum purchase and sale agreements, priced at prevailing market rates, to support long-term sourcing and non-U.S. business needs. These were accounting derivatives; they expired by December 31, 2025, leaving no notional amounts.

nodes.title: Notional Amounts and Fair Values
nodes.summary: The text reports derivative notional amounts and fair values at December 31, 2025 and 2024, including hedge-designated and undesignated contracts, accrued liabilities, other assets, and netting. It summarizes hedge gains and losses recognized in other comprehensive income and reclassified from AOCI to earnings by contract type and income-statement category, notes insignificant gains or losses on undesignated derivatives, and expects $16 million pre-tax of hedge gains to be reclassified within 12 months. It describes derivative credit-risk contingencies, a $3 million net liability subject to settlement, and no collateral posted. It also explains the three-level fair value hierarchy, lists recurring fair-value assets and liabilities for 2025 and 2024 by level, and describes valuation methods for investments and foreign-currency and commodity derivatives.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements and Derivative Risks
nodes.summary: Describes expected reclassification of $16 million in pre-tax cash flow hedge gains from AOCI to earnings over the next 12 months, and derivative credit-risk contingencies, including potential settlement or collateral requirements; no collateral was posted at year-end 2025. Defines the three fair value hierarchy levels and lists recurring fair-value assets: money market funds, available-for-sale commercial paper, corporate notes and U.S. government agency securities, other equity investments, and derivatives.

nodes.title: Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text presents fair-value hierarchy data for liabilities and derivatives at December 31, 2025 and 2024, and valuation methods for money-market funds, investments, and foreign-currency and commodity derivatives. It reports nonrecurring impairment losses and related fair values for property, plant and equipment, investments, other assets, and operating-lease equipment, explaining the valuation methods and management reviews used. It also compares carrying amounts with fair values and hierarchy levels for notes receivable and debt, excluding finance lease obligations, for both dates.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures
nodes.summary: Reports nonrecurring fair value impairment losses and related asset values for 2025 and 2024, with valuation methods for investments, other assets, property and equipment, and operating lease equipment. It also compares carrying amounts and fair values of notes receivable and debt, excluding finance lease obligations, at December 31, 2025 and 2024, with fair values by hierarchy level.

nodes.title: Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text reports nonrecurring impairment losses and fair values for long-lived assets in 2025 and 2024, and explains valuation methods for investments, other assets, property and equipment, and operating lease equipment. It also presents carrying amounts and fair values of notes receivable and debt at both year-ends, their fair-value hierarchy levels and estimation methods. Fair values of indemnifications and financing commitments cannot practicably be estimated; omitted financial instruments generally have carrying values approximating fair value, using Level 2 inputs except cash, which is Level 1.

nodes.title: Note 23 – Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: Boeing faces a broad range of business-related lawsuits, claims, and government investigations that may lead to financial penalties or restrictions on government contracting, certifications, or exports. A May 2025 agreement with the Department of Justice over the 737 MAX crashes requires a $244 million fine and $445 million for victims’ families, both held in escrow; a court approved dismissal of the criminal case in November 2025, but families’ representatives appealed. Other MAX-related civil and securities cases remain pending, as do investigations and lawsuits arising from the January 2024 737-9 door-plug accident. Boeing cannot reasonably estimate uninsured losses beyond accrued amounts.

nodes.title: Note 24 – Segment and Revenue Information
nodes.summary: Note 24 describes the company’s three reportable segments—BCA, BDS and BGS—and other activities classified as unallocated items, eliminations and other, with segment-data details referenced on page 59. It outlines each segment’s products and services and revenue-recognition timing: BCA aircraft and BGS spare parts at delivery or acceptance, and most BDS and other BGS contracts over time as costs are incurred. The CEO is the chief operating decision maker and uses segment operating earnings or losses to allocate resources and monitor performance against prior periods, forecasts and the annual plan. A table reconciles segment revenue to operating earnings or losses for 2023 and 2024, deducting research and development expense and other segment items.

nodes.title: For the year ended December 31, 2025
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023–2025 segment revenues and operating earnings/losses for BCA, BDS and BGS, with notes on other segment costs and a divestiture gain. It details consolidated and segment revenues by customer geography, contract category and revenue-recognition method; U.S. government revenue shares and overseas operating assets; equity-method investment income; and backlog value, expected conversion, timing uncertainty and cancellation risks. It also explains unallocated costs, intersegment eliminations and cost allocation.

nodes.title: BGS Revenue, Equity Earnings, Backlog and Allocations
nodes.summary: BGS revenues for 2023–2025 are broken down by commercial and government customers, intersegment eliminations, and total revenue, with percentages for point-in-time recognition, fixed-price contracts, and U.S. government revenue (including FMS). Equity-method income was $33 million in 2025, $104 million in 2024, and $70 million in 2023, primarily from BDS investments. Backlog was $682.207 billion at year-end 2025; about 13% is expected to convert by 2026 and 55% by 2029, though timing is uncertain and delays or disruptions may reduce or cancel orders. Unallocated items cover shared services, intersegment eliminations, and costs generally allocated under U.S. Government CAS.

nodes.title: Unallocated Items, Eliminations and other
nodes.summary: The text reports BGS revenues for 2023–2025 by commercial and government customers, total and intersegment revenues, and percentages recognized at a point in time, on fixed-price contracts, and from the U.S. government (including FMS). It gives equity-method investment income and notes BDS was the primary contributor. It describes backlog of $682.207 billion at year-end 2025, expected revenue conversion through 2026 and 2029, and risks of delays or cancellations. It explains unallocated costs and eliminations, lists their components and annual totals for 2023–2025, and notes DOJ-related earnings charges in 2024 and 2025.

nodes.title: Pension and Other Postretirement Benefit Expense
nodes.summary: Pension costs for BDS and BGS government-customer work are allocated under CAS, which uses assumptions and conventions differing from GAAP; other postretirement costs are allocated to segments under CAS, generally based on benefits paid. The FAS/CAS service cost adjustment is the difference between GAAP service costs and costs allocated to segments. Non-operating benefit expenses comprise net periodic benefit costs other than service cost and are included in Other income, net. nodes.title: Cost Estimates for Fixed-Price Development Contracts — Refer to Notes 1 and 15 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns uncertain cost-to-complete and margin estimates for fixed-price development contracts, which drive revenue recognized over time using costs incurred. Complex programs, limited historical data, supply-chain and operational inefficiencies, and significant judgment create risk of reduced margins or reach-forward losses and require specialized audit expertise. Auditors assessed estimation methods, assumptions, outcomes and estimate-change timing; interviewed project personnel; observed work sites; tested data and developed independent expectations; reviewed prior estimates against actual results; and tested related controls.

nodes.title: Program Accounting Estimates for the 777X program — Refer to Notes 1 and 9 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns Boeing’s 777X program accounting estimates. Because no aircraft have been delivered, costs are recognized only if estimated program costs exceed revenue; Boeing recorded about $4.9 billion in reach-forward losses in 2025. Production challenges and certification delays make schedules, costs, program margins, and customer consideration estimates highly uncertain and could cause further material losses. Auditing these estimates required extensive effort, judgment, and industry expertise. Auditors assessed management’s methods, assumptions, and estimates; interviewed personnel about program status and customer negotiations; reviewed regulator communications and external reports; evaluated certification schedules, production costs, and prior forecasting accuracy; compared customer consideration estimates with historical outcomes and communications; and tested related controls, data, calculations, and judgments.

nodes.title: Program Accounting Estimates for the 737 program — Refer to Notes 1 and 9 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The text describes the 737 program accounting estimate as a critical audit matter: uncertainty in production rates, FAA oversight, and management’s cost and revenue judgments made auditing complex. Deloitte’s procedures included production-line and management inquiries, review of FAA communications and safety metrics, research for delay indicators, schedule reasonableness and historical-output analysis, and internal-control testing. Deloitte signed its report in Seattle on January 30, 2026, noting service as auditor since at least 1934. Its separate report found Boeing’s internal controls over financial reporting effective in all material respects as of December 31, 2025, excluding newly acquired Spirit AeroSystems. It explains management and auditor responsibilities, audit standards and procedures, and the purpose and limitations of internal controls.

The audit excluded Spirit AeroSystems, acquired December 8, 2025, which represented about 9% of assets and under 1% of revenues and operating earnings. Management is responsible for controls and its assessment; the auditor describes its PCAOB independence and audit procedures, which provided reasonable assurance and a basis for its opinion.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Defines internal control over financial reporting as a process providing reasonable assurance of reliable external financial statements under GAAP. It includes policies for accurate records, authorized and properly recorded transactions and expenditures, and preventing or timely detecting asset misuse with potentially material effects. Controls cannot guarantee prevention or detection of misstatements, and future effectiveness may decline due to changing conditions or reduced compliance. The section is signed by Deloitte & Touche LLP in Seattle on January 30, 2026.

title: The Boeing Company Global Annual Incentive Plan

nodes.title: Section 1. Purpose of the Plan
nodes.summary: Exhibit 10.9 presents Boeing’s Global Annual Incentive Plan, amended and restated effective January 1, 2026. The plan aims to attract and retain executives, managers, and individual contributors by rewarding performance that advances business objectives and linking employee contributions to overall company performance. It consolidates and replaces three prior Boeing incentive plans.

nodes.title: Section 2. Terms and Definitions
nodes.summary: Defines Plan-specific terminology: Board, Committee, Company (including adopting affiliates), Bonus Factor, Company Performance Score, Performance Goals, Incentive-Eligible Pay, and Incentive Award Target, with several terms specified in appendices or other sections. Eligible Employees are regular-payroll employees meeting Section 3 criteria, including approved-leave employees, but exclude special-fee or contract workers, contractors, temporary or hourly special employees, and collectively represented employees; the administrator decides eligibility uniformly and without discrimination. Awards depend on targets, performance scores, bonus factors, and adjustments, and are capped at twice target; targets are capped at twice applicable base salary. Also defines Performance Period, administrator authority by employee category, Qualifying Termination events (specified retirement, death, disability, or layoff), and the compensation vice president role.

nodes.title: Section 3. Eligibility and Administration
nodes.summary: The text sets eligibility rules, including active-payroll service, exclusions for participation in another Company Performance Score-based plan, administrator authority to exclude groups, and possible award proration for changing appendices or targets, qualifying termination, leave, or hire/rehire. The Committee sets performance goals, achievement ranges, and scores at its discretion, then determines awards using applicable appendix formulas. Awards are generally paid in a lump sum promptly, subject to U.S. timing limits and permitted deferral; non-qualifying prepayment termination forfeits awards. The administrator may determine treatment after corporate transactions and grant minimum payouts. The Board or Committee may amend or terminate the Plan at any time.

nodes.title: Performance Scoring and Incentive Awards
key_items: Section 4. Determination of Company Performance Score
Section 5. Determination and Payment of Incentive Awards
nodes.summary: The Plan Administrator may exclude employee groups from participation. The Committee sets performance goals and achievement ranges within the first three months of each period, may tailor them by employee group, and determines scores at its discretion. At period-end, it assesses results and calculates awards under applicable formulas; awards are generally paid in a lump sum promptly, subject to deferral rules and a U.S. deadline. Employees terminated before payment other than in a Qualifying Termination forfeit awards. The Plan Administrator also determines award treatment after specified corporate transactions and may guarantee minimum payouts.

nodes.title: Section 6. General Provisions
nodes.summary: The Plan may be amended or terminated at any time by the Board or Committee; the Plan Administrator interprets it, and administrator and committee decisions are final. Awards are subject to required tax withholding and permitted Company deductions, cannot be transferred or attached, and earn no interest. The Plan grants no employment rights. Compensation is intended to comply with or qualify for Code Section 409A exemptions, including applicable short-term deferral timing. Layoff-plan benefits replace, rather than supplement, Plan awards. Payments for incapacitated employees may go to their caregiver or institution. Delaware law governs unless federal law applies, and the Plan prevails over conflicting award documents. Awards for employees outside the U.S. must comply with local requirements, with the Administrator authorized to adapt them.

summary: The Boeing Global Annual Incentive Plan, amended effective January 1, 2026, replaces three prior plans and rewards eligible employees for performance supporting business objectives. It defines key terms, eligibility and exclusions, award targets and caps, performance periods, qualifying terminations, and administrator roles. The Committee sets goals and scores and determines awards under applicable formulas; awards may be prorated, adjusted for transactions, or subject to minimum payouts, and are generally paid promptly, with forfeiture rules and permitted deferrals. The plan also covers amendment and administration, taxes, transfer restrictions, employment rights, 409A compliance, layoff benefits, incapacitated employees, governing law, conflicting documents, and adaptations for non-U.S. employees.

title: Appendix A
summary: Appendix A sets executive incentive rules: awards generally equal the target multiplied by the Company Performance Score and individual Bonus Factor. It defines who assigns performance factors and targets for elected and other executives, and how eligible pay is determined, including for qualifying terminations. Awards are subject to the Board’s Clawback Policy and forfeiture or recovery for specified misconduct within two years of the later of vesting or payment, subject to local law; future compensation may be offset. Acceptance acknowledges these conditions, with protections for legally protected communications and testimony. The CHRO may approve and document enforceability-related modifications. Committee and/or Board control all decisions on elected executives’ participation.

title: Appendix B
summary: Appendix B sets out the Global Annual Incentive Plan rules for employees serving in non-executive management roles during any part of a performance period. A manager’s award equals the incentive target multiplied by the Company Performance Score and the manager’s Bonus Factor. The Bonus Factor reflects an individual performance evaluation under Plan Administrator-approved procedures. Targets may be a percentage of eligible pay or a fixed local-currency amount, set by manager level and relevant organizational or market criteria. Eligible pay is annual base pay on a Plan Administrator-designated fourth-quarter cut-off date, or, for managers who leave earlier, their base pay on the termination date.

summary: Appendix C applies to eligible non-executive, non-manager individual contributors during any portion of a performance period. Their incentive award equals the target multiplied by the Company Performance Score and an individually assigned performance-based Bonus Factor. It defines the Bonus Factor, target (which may vary by location, unit, function, level, or other criteria), and Incentive-Eligible Pay, subject to Plan Administrator adjustments. title: Amendment No. 1 to the Supplemental Executive Retirement Plan for Employees of The Boeing Company (As Amended and Restated as of June 1, 2021)
summary: Amendment No. 1, effective October 31, 2025, changes Boeing’s Supplemental Executive Retirement Plan. Employees transferred under the Jupiter Agreement are not treated as separated from service until they terminate employment with the buyer and its affiliates. For separations after normal retirement age, target benefits include compensation and service before and after that age, while offset benefits reflect late retirement under the PVP. Early-retirement benefits reduce the target benefit by 0.25% per month before age 62; vested terminated benefits for participants not yet eligible for PVP early retirement reduce it by 0.5% per month before age 65. In both cases, the offset is adjusted for single-life-annuity payments beginning at the participant’s commencement date under PVP rules.
